summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the last surviving sodomy provisions is concluded, and the criminal code as it now stands contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct. Those provisions reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no corresponding offence for heterosexual acts. Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy guarantees.

Policing of same-sex affection has run through public-order law rather than a sodomy statute. A former provision criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Visible, politically active LGBTQ signage is frequently a target of government crackdowns, at times with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender or name on identity documents. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree allowing 35 transgender Dominicans to change their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35 and subsequently changed her name. No standing procedure for legal gender recognition exists. A 2017 ILGA poll found 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Family law recognises no legal status between persons of the same sex, neither marriage nor a civil or domestic partnership. Article 55, added by the 2010 constitutional amendment, provides that the State promotes and protects family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, constitutionally barring same-sex marriage; households headed by such couples are excluded from the rights granted to married opposite-sex couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on private international law could justify recognition, since a marriage is valid if the law of the place of celebration, or the national law or domicile of at least one spouse, treats it as such. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems, including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it. A trans visitor in a relationship that Dominican law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls outside this framework, whatever the couple's own documents record.

Access to health care is a constitutional right, but health programmes for the LGBTQ community have generally concentrated on HIV/AIDS education and are largely run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services or public accommodations. The one sector-specific provision is Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS, in force since 2011, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations carry significant weight in public policy and in prevailing attitudes. The major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals.
tangentialFactors:
United States Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster, openly gay, served in Santo Domingo from 2013 to 2017. Religious leaders and some politicians regularly insulted him after his June 2015 presentation with his husband, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him. His departure in 2017 left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence that included speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016.

In April 2017 more than 300 activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo, where Dominican government officials spoke.
localsOnly:
For residents, the absence of discrimination protection in employment, housing, banking, transportation and government services means many LGBTQ Dominicans keep their identity concealed.

Community infrastructure centres on HIV services and sex-worker organising. COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, was co-founded in 2004 and is led by trans sex workers; HIV/AIDS education and support is delivered by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos.

A name change to match gender identity has required an executive decree covering named individuals rather than a standing administrative procedure, so transgender residents have no routine route to documents that match how they live.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Universal Periodic Review record shows the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on the rights of intersex persons and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. No domestic implementing measure for those commitments appears in the sources reviewed.

Whether Article 41 of Law 544-14 is applied by Dominican registries or courts to recognise a marriage validly celebrated abroad is not established in the sources, and it stands against the constitutional bar in Article 55.

Implementation of the January 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion remains unresolved: legal experts say the country must apply it, but no legislation or judgment giving effect to it is sourced.

The inventory contains no hate-crime provision, no sentencing enhancement, and no documented enforcement data for offences against transgender people; whether such protections exist is not established by the sources reviewed.
